Ella suggested waiting and watching instead. The next morning, a small bird landed near the quiet corner. Ella made a note of the time before refilling the bowl.

For four mornings, Ella watched from inside the window. She recorded the time, the weather and whether a bird visited. On the fourth morning, two birds arrived together. Ben wanted to announce that the bowl was a success. Ella pointed out that four days were only a small sample. They had not watched every hour, and they could not know whether the same birds returned. They decided to keep observing without disturbing the visitors. Ella asked an adult to help clean the bowl each evening and replace the water. Ben drew a simple chart with room for another week of observations.

items.prompt: Who is the main character in “The garden gate”?

stimuli.text:
Mina noticed that the community garden gate was open. A small rabbit was nibbling the lettuce inside. She could not see the gardener. Mina closed the gate gently after guiding the rabbit outside with a trail of leaves. Then she waited beside the fence. When the gardener arrived, she explained what had happened. He thanked her for protecting the plants without frightening the rabbit.

The next Saturday, Mina returned to help plant beans. Before she started, she checked the latch. It slid into place but slipped out again when she pushed the gate. Now she understood why the rabbit had entered. The gardener, Tomas, brought a small toolbox. He showed Mina the loose screw holding the latch to the post. She held the metal plate steady while he tightened it. They tested the gate together three times. Each time it stayed shut. Mina wrote a short note asking visitors to check the latch as they left. She drew a rabbit beside the words, hoping the picture would remind people why the gate mattered.

hints: Locate the matching detail in the passage.

items.explanation: The answer is Mina. Locate the matching detail in the passage.

items.prompt: Who is the main character in “The lantern walk”?

stimuli.text:
Arun was making a lantern for the neighbourhood walk. His first paper cover tore when he pulled it over the frame. He wanted to throw it away. His sister Jo suggested using the torn paper to practise a smaller fold. Arun tried again more slowly. The new cover fitted. He saved the scraps in a box for someone else to use.

On the evening of the walk, a gust of wind lifted several decorations from the meeting table. Arun held his lantern close while Jo gathered the loose paper. A younger child named Bea stared at her empty frame. Her cover had blown into a puddle. Arun remembered the box of scraps at home. He could not fetch it before the walk began, but Jo had kept some spare pieces in her bag. Together they made a patchwork cover. Bea chose a blue triangle for the window and a yellow circle for the moon. It looked different from the other lanterns, which pleased her.

items.explanation: The answer is Arun. Locate the matching detail in the passage.

items.title: Compare
items.prompt: How do the sources differ?

stimuli.text:
Source A. Watching a Water Bowl. Ella, neighbourhood observation notebook, 15 October. Fictional practice source.
Ella watched a clean water bowl from the same window for ten minutes on each of five mornings. She recorded three bird visits on Monday, four on Tuesday, three on Wednesday, five on Thursday and five on Friday. There were twenty visits in the observation periods. She did not mark individual birds, so the notes cannot show how many different birds visited. A bird could have returned more than once.
The bowl stood in a shaded corner. An adult cleaned it and replaced the water each evening. Ella kept the location and observation time the same during the five days. She also noted that all five mornings were warm. Her notebook does not compare warm weather with cold weather or this balcony with other locations.
Ella concludes that birds visited this particular bowl during the recorded periods. She suggests watching for another week before making claims about a pattern. She would also like to compare observations at different times of day. Her record explains what she counted and what she did not know. Other observers could repeat the method, although their results might differ. The notebook provides a small, direct observation rather than proof that every bird needs the same arrangement.

Source B. The Wonderful Bird Bowl. Promotional leaflet from a fictional garden shop, 16 October. Fictional practice source.
Our wonderful bird bowl is the only bowl your garden will ever need! A neighbour saw birds drinking from a bowl just like ours. That means this product will bring birds to every balcony, in every season. There is no need to compare locations or wait for more observations. Twenty visits must mean twenty different birds, and every visitor will certainly return tomorrow.
The leaflet shows a bright picture of a bird beside a bowl. It gives the shop's opening hours and explains how to order the product. It does not provide a description of the balcony, the weather, the time spent watching or how the visits were counted. No comparison with other bowls is included. The author sells the product and wants readers to buy it.
A large heading calls the bowl a guaranteed success. Smaller print says that the picture is an illustration and that garden conditions vary. Those details do not support the guarantee in the heading. Readers can separate the useful product information from the claims about bird behaviour. They could ask for evidence, compare independent observations and consider what cleaning or placement is needed. Enthusiastic wording can attract attention, but enthusiasm does not turn an untested promise into a reliable conclusion.

items.title: Compare
items.prompt: How do the sources differ?

stimuli.text:
Source A. Testing a Garden Handle. Mina and Leena, design trial notes, 18 October. Fictional practice source.
The garden team tried three temporary gate handles. Eight volunteer visitors tested each design while the gate was supervised. The team recorded whether each visitor could reach and grip the handle and whether the gate latched after use. They did not ask visitors to give a score for how attractive the handle looked.
The first design caught one person's sleeve. Two visitors found the second design difficult to grip. Everyone in this small group could reach and grip the third design. The team checked its latch three times and found it closed each time. These observations helped them choose a design for a longer trial. They did not prove that it would suit every visitor or remain reliable through every season.
The notes include a sketch and explain the testing steps. They also name two questions for later: whether rain makes the handle slippery and whether visitors using different mobility aids can use it comfortably. The volunteers were available on one afternoon, so the group might not represent all garden users. Mina and Leena recommend inviting more visitors before making a permanent change. Their report combines a useful comparison with clear limits. It gives readers enough detail to understand the decision and to suggest what should be tested next.

Source B. A Perfect Gate for Everyone. Promotional announcement from a fictional handle supplier, 19 October. Fictional practice source.
Choose our new garden handle and solve every access problem at once! A small group tried a similar design and everyone managed to use it. Our announcement therefore calls this handle perfect for every person, every gate and every kind of weather. It says no further testing is necessary because a successful afternoon tells us everything we need to know.
The announcement includes a photograph of a smiling visitor and a large button inviting readers to place an order. It lists the colour choices and price. Those details are useful when comparing products, but they do not establish the universal access claim. The supplier does not explain whether its handle has the same dimensions or mechanism as the tested model. It provides no record of use in rain or over a long period.
Readers should distinguish the eight visitors' recorded experiences from the supplier's much broader promise. A product can perform well in a small trial while still needing further checks. The announcement has a commercial purpose and selects the most positive part of the report. A careful reader could ask for the original notes, look for independent testing and include more users in a local trial. Recognising this purpose helps readers judge the claim without dismissing every product detail.

items.title: Compare
items.prompt: How do the sources differ?

stimuli.text:
Source A. Comparing Paper Covers. Jo, craft group test record, 20 October. Fictional practice source.
The craft group compared four folded covers with four patchwork covers for battery lanterns. They used the same frame size and dry paper from the same pack. An adult placed each finished cover beside the same fan for three minutes. The group recorded whether a seam opened or the paper tore. This was a classroom-style material comparison, not a safety certification.
One folded cover tore at a corner. None of the four patchwork covers tore during the short test. The record also notes that the patchwork covers took longer to assemble and used more tape. The group kept the damaged cover to examine the torn corner. Jo suggests that strengthening a fold might change the result, so the shape of a cover is not the only possible explanation.
The record describes what happened under these particular conditions. It does not test rain, strong outdoor gusts or repeated use. Four examples of each design are a small sample. The group recommends trying more covers before deciding which design is more durable. Its notes are useful because they describe materials, method and observations as well as questions. Another group could repeat the comparison and record whether its results agree. Neither design should be described as unbreakable on the strength of this test.

Source B. Lanterns That Last Forever. Promotional poster from a fictional craft seller, 21 October. Fictional practice source.
Our patchwork lantern covers never tear! A craft group tried a few paper covers near a fan and none of its patchwork examples broke. Our poster turns that short observation into a promise that every patchwork cover will last forever. The headline gives no conditions and does not mention the small number tested. It also leaves out the extra time and tape needed to make the covers.
The poster offers colourful paper packs and shows three attractive finished lanterns. It tells readers the price and how to join a workshop. It does not show the test record or explain whether the pictured covers use the same paper, tape or frame. The seller benefits if people choose the advertised design, so the purpose of the poster matters when evaluating its language.
A reader can enjoy the design without accepting an unsupported guarantee. The short test suggests a question worth investigating, but it cannot predict every future use. Rain, repeated handling and different construction methods could produce other results. Comparing the poster with the original record reveals the difference between an observed outcome and a universal claim. Asking for details and looking for further evidence are useful next steps before treating a cheerful slogan as a dependable promise.

stimuli.text:
Source A. Comparing Paper Covers. Jo, craft group test record, 20 October. Fictional practice source.
The craft group compared four folded covers with four patchwork covers for battery lanterns. They used the same frame size and dry paper from the same pack. An adult placed each finished cover beside the same fan for three minutes. The group recorded whether a seam opened or the paper tore. This was a classroom-style material comparison, not a safety certification.
One folded cover tore at a corner. None of the four patchwork covers tore during the short test. The record also notes that the patchwork covers took longer to assemble and used more tape. The group kept the damaged cover to examine the torn corner. Jo suggests that strengthening a fold might change the result, so the shape of a cover is not the only possible explanation.
The record describes what happened under these particular conditions. It does not test rain, strong outdoor gusts or repeated use. Four examples of each design are a small sample. The group recommends trying more covers before deciding which design is more durable. Its notes are useful because they describe materials, method and observations as well as questions. Another group could repeat the comparison and record whether its results agree. Neither design should be described as unbreakable on the strength of this test.

Source B. Lanterns That Last Forever. Promotional poster from a fictional craft seller, 21 October. Fictional practice source.
Our patchwork lantern covers never tear! A craft group tried a few paper covers near a fan and none of its patchwork examples broke. Our poster turns that short observation into a promise that every patchwork cover will last forever. The headline gives no conditions and does not mention the small number tested. It also leaves out the extra time and tape needed to make the covers.
The poster offers colourful paper packs and shows three attractive finished lanterns. It tells readers the price and how to join a workshop. It does not show the test record or explain whether the pictured covers use the same paper, tape or frame. The seller benefits if people choose the advertised design, so the purpose of the poster matters when evaluating its language.
A reader can enjoy the design without accepting an unsupported guarantee. The short test suggests a question worth investigating, but it cannot predict every future use. Rain, repeated handling and different construction methods could produce other results. Comparing the poster with the original record reveals the difference between an observed outcome and a universal claim. Asking for details and looking for further evidence are useful next steps before treating a cheerful slogan as a dependable promise.

items.title: Reliability
items.prompt: Which source gives a clearer basis for checking the claim?

stimuli.text:
Source A. Watching a Water Bowl. Ella, neighbourhood observation notebook, 15 October. Fictional practice source.
Ella watched a clean water bowl from the same window for ten minutes on each of five mornings. She recorded three bird visits on Monday, four on Tuesday, three on Wednesday, five on Thursday and five on Friday. There were twenty visits in the observation periods. She did not mark individual birds, so the notes cannot show how many different birds visited. A bird could have returned more than once.
The bowl stood in a shaded corner. An adult cleaned it and replaced the water each evening. Ella kept the location and observation time the same during the five days. She also noted that all five mornings were warm. Her notebook does not compare warm weather with cold weather or this balcony with other locations.
Ella concludes that birds visited this particular bowl during the recorded periods. She suggests watching for another week before making claims about a pattern. She would also like to compare observations at different times of day. Her record explains what she counted and what she did not know. Other observers could repeat the method, although their results might differ. The notebook provides a small, direct observation rather than proof that every bird needs the same arrangement.

Source B. The Wonderful Bird Bowl. Promotional leaflet from a fictional garden shop, 16 October. Fictional practice source.
Our wonderful bird bowl is the only bowl your garden will ever need! A neighbour saw birds drinking from a bowl just like ours. That means this product will bring birds to every balcony, in every season. There is no need to compare locations or wait for more observations. Twenty visits must mean twenty different birds, and every visitor will certainly return tomorrow.
The leaflet shows a bright picture of a bird beside a bowl. It gives the shop's opening hours and explains how to order the product. It does not provide a description of the balcony, the weather, the time spent watching or how the visits were counted. No comparison with other bowls is included. The author sells the product and wants readers to buy it.
A large heading calls the bowl a guaranteed success. Smaller print says that the picture is an illustration and that garden conditions vary. Those details do not support the guarantee in the heading. Readers can separate the useful product information from the claims about bird behaviour. They could ask for evidence, compare independent observations and consider what cleaning or placement is needed. Enthusiastic wording can attract attention, but enthusiasm does not turn an untested promise into a reliable conclusion.

items.prompt: Which source gives a clearer basis for checking the claim?

stimuli.text:
Source A. Testing a Garden Handle. Mina and Leena, design trial notes, 18 October. Fictional practice source.
The garden team tried three temporary gate handles. Eight volunteer visitors tested each design while the gate was supervised. The team recorded whether each visitor could reach and grip the handle and whether the gate latched after use. They did not ask visitors to give a score for how attractive the handle looked.
The first design caught one person's sleeve. Two visitors found the second design difficult to grip. Everyone in this small group could reach and grip the third design. The team checked its latch three times and found it closed each time. These observations helped them choose a design for a longer trial. They did not prove that it would suit every visitor or remain reliable through every season.
The notes include a sketch and explain the testing steps. They also name two questions for later: whether rain makes the handle slippery and whether visitors using different mobility aids can use it comfortably. The volunteers were available on one afternoon, so the group might not represent all garden users. Mina and Leena recommend inviting more visitors before making a permanent change. Their report combines a useful comparison with clear limits. It gives readers enough detail to understand the decision and to suggest what should be tested next.

Source B. A Perfect Gate for Everyone. Promotional announcement from a fictional handle supplier, 19 October. Fictional practice source.
Choose our new garden handle and solve every access problem at once! A small group tried a similar design and everyone managed to use it. Our announcement therefore calls this handle perfect for every person, every gate and every kind of weather. It says no further testing is necessary because a successful afternoon tells us everything we need to know.
The announcement includes a photograph of a smiling visitor and a large button inviting readers to place an order. It lists the colour choices and price. Those details are useful when comparing products, but they do not establish the universal access claim. The supplier does not explain whether its handle has the same dimensions or mechanism as the tested model. It provides no record of use in rain or over a long period.
Readers should distinguish the eight visitors' recorded experiences from the supplier's much broader promise. A product can perform well in a small trial while still needing further checks. The announcement has a commercial purpose and selects the most positive part of the report. A careful reader could ask for the original notes, look for independent testing and include more users in a local trial. Recognising this purpose helps readers judge the claim without dismissing every product detail.

stimuli.text:
Mina noticed that the community garden gate was open. A small rabbit was nibbling the lettuce inside. She could not see the gardener. Mina closed the gate gently after guiding the rabbit outside with a trail of leaves. Then she waited beside the fence. When the gardener arrived, she explained what had happened. He thanked her for protecting the plants without frightening the rabbit.

The next Saturday, Mina returned to help plant beans. Before she started, she checked the latch. It slid into place but slipped out again when she pushed the gate. Now she understood why the rabbit had entered. The gardener, Tomas, brought a small toolbox. He showed Mina the loose screw holding the latch to the post. She held the metal plate steady while he tightened it. They tested the gate together three times. Each time it stayed shut. Mina wrote a short note asking visitors to check the latch as they left. She drew a rabbit beside the words, hoping the picture would remind people why the gate mattered.

A week later, Mina found a new problem. A visitor using a wheelchair had difficulty reaching the high latch. The visitor, Leena, could push the gate easily once it was open, but she needed someone else to let her through. Mina felt pleased with the repair until Leena explained this. A gate that kept rabbits out also needed to welcome every gardener.

Mina asked Tomas whether they could simply lower the latch. He explained that a low latch might be easy for younger children to open without an adult. They needed to consider more than one person's needs. Leena suggested a longer handle connected to the existing mechanism. Tomas sketched the idea on the back of an old seed packet. Mina measured the gate while Leena tried different handle positions using a strip of cardboard.

stimuli.text:
Arun was making a lantern for the neighbourhood walk. His first paper cover tore when he pulled it over the frame. He wanted to throw it away. His sister Jo suggested using the torn paper to practise a smaller fold. Arun tried again more slowly. The new cover fitted. He saved the scraps in a box for someone else to use.

On the evening of the walk, a gust of wind lifted several decorations from the meeting table. Arun held his lantern close while Jo gathered the loose paper. A younger child named Bea stared at her empty frame. Her cover had blown into a puddle. Arun remembered the box of scraps at home. He could not fetch it before the walk began, but Jo had kept some spare pieces in her bag. Together they made a patchwork cover. Bea chose a blue triangle for the window and a yellow circle for the moon. It looked different from the other lanterns, which pleased her.

The organisers announced that the group would follow the riverside path. Arun had practised carrying his lantern along the short route behind his house. The riverside walk was longer, and the wind was stronger there. He asked whether Bea would manage with her repaired cover. Bea said she wanted to try, but she would like to stay near someone she knew.

As they walked, Arun watched the blue and yellow patches glow around the small battery light. He had wanted his own lantern to look perfect. Now he noticed how many different designs surrounded him. One had painted leaves. Another had a crooked star. An older neighbour carried a plain jar that caught reflections from every passing light.

At the narrow bridge, the group slowed down. Someone behind Arun called for everyone to hurry. Jo asked them to wait while a family crossed safely. Bea held her lantern in both hands and watched the water below. Arun stood beside her rather than pulling her forward. When she was ready, they walked across at her pace.

stimuli.text:
Ella put a bowl of water on the balcony during a hot week. No birds visited on the first day. Her cousin Ben thought they should move it beside the noisy doorway. Ella suggested waiting and watching instead. The next morning, a small bird landed near the quiet corner. Ella made a note of the time before refilling the bowl.

For four mornings, Ella watched from inside the window. She recorded the time, the weather and whether a bird visited. On the fourth morning, two birds arrived together. Ben wanted to announce that the bowl was a success. Ella pointed out that four days were only a small sample. They had not watched every hour, and they could not know whether the same birds returned. They decided to keep observing without disturbing the visitors. Ella asked an adult to help clean the bowl each evening and replace the water. Ben drew a simple chart with room for another week of observations.

Their neighbour Samira noticed the chart when she came to visit. She explained that birds also needed shelter from predators and a clear view of their surroundings. A bowl could be clean and full yet still be in an unsuitable place. Ella showed her the quiet corner. A tall pot partly blocked the view from one side. With an adult's help, they moved the pot away without shifting the water bowl.

The following week was cooler. Fewer birds appeared in the mornings. Ben wondered whether moving the pot had caused the change. Ella looked at the weather notes. Perhaps the birds needed less water in cooler conditions, or perhaps they were visiting at another time. Their chart could suggest questions, but it could not answer all of them. They added a short afternoon observation on the weekend.

When their class began a project about helping local wildlife, Ben wanted to use a large heading that said their balcony had saved dozens of birds. Ella disagreed. They had counted visits, not individual birds, and had no evidence that any bird had been in danger. Samira helped them choose a more accurate heading: Watching Birds at a Balcony Water Bowl. Under it, they described what they had done and what they still did not know.

stimuli.text:

items.title: Language effect
items.prompt: What effect do the described actions have?

stimuli.text:
Ella put a bowl of water on the balcony during a hot week. No birds visited on the first day. Her cousin Ben thought they should move it beside the noisy doorway. Ella suggested waiting and watching instead. The next morning, a small bird landed near the quiet corner. Ella made a note of the time before refilling the bowl.

For four mornings, Ella watched from inside the window. She recorded the time, the weather and whether a bird visited. On the fourth morning, two birds arrived together. Ben wanted to announce that the bowl was a success. Ella pointed out that four days were only a small sample. They had not watched every hour, and they could not know whether the same birds returned. They decided to keep observing without disturbing the visitors. Ella asked an adult to help clean the bowl each evening and replace the water. Ben drew a simple chart with room for another week of observations.

Their neighbour Samira noticed the chart when she came to visit. She explained that birds also needed shelter from predators and a clear view of their surroundings. A bowl could be clean and full yet still be in an unsuitable place. Ella showed her the quiet corner. A tall pot partly blocked the view from one side. With an adult's help, they moved the pot away without shifting the water bowl.

The following week was cooler. Fewer birds appeared in the mornings. Ben wondered whether moving the pot had caused the change. Ella looked at the weather notes. Perhaps the birds needed less water in cooler conditions, or perhaps they were visiting at another time. Their chart could suggest questions, but it could not answer all of them. They added a short afternoon observation on the weekend.

When their class began a project about helping local wildlife, Ben wanted to use a large heading that said their balcony had saved dozens of birds. Ella disagreed. They had counted visits, not individual birds, and had no evidence that any bird had been in danger. Samira helped them choose a more accurate heading: Watching Birds at a Balcony Water Bowl. Under it, they described what they had done and what they still did not know.

items.title: Synthesise
items.prompt: What conclusion follows when both sources are considered?

stimuli.text:
Source A. Testing a Garden Handle. Mina and Leena, design trial notes, 18 October. Fictional practice source.
The garden team tried three temporary gate handles. Eight volunteer visitors tested each design while the gate was supervised. The team recorded whether each visitor could reach and grip the handle and whether the gate latched after use. They did not ask visitors to give a score for how attractive the handle looked.
The first design caught one person's sleeve. Two visitors found the second design difficult to grip. Everyone in this small group could reach and grip the third design. The team checked its latch three times and found it closed each time. These observations helped them choose a design for a longer trial. They did not prove that it would suit every visitor or remain reliable through every season.
The notes include a sketch and explain the testing steps. They also name two questions for later: whether rain makes the handle slippery and whether visitors using different mobility aids can use it comfortably. The volunteers were available on one afternoon, so the group might not represent all garden users. Mina and Leena recommend inviting more visitors before making a permanent change. Their report combines a useful comparison with clear limits. It gives readers enough detail to understand the decision and to suggest what should be tested next.

Source B. A Perfect Gate for Everyone. Promotional announcement from a fictional handle supplier, 19 October. Fictional practice source.
Choose our new garden handle and solve every access problem at once! A small group tried a similar design and everyone managed to use it. Our announcement therefore calls this handle perfect for every person, every gate and every kind of weather. It says no further testing is necessary because a successful afternoon tells us everything we need to know.
The announcement includes a photograph of a smiling visitor and a large button inviting readers to place an order. It lists the colour choices and price. Those details are useful when comparing products, but they do not establish the universal access claim. The supplier does not explain whether its handle has the same dimensions or mechanism as the tested model. It provides no record of use in rain or over a long period.
Readers should distinguish the eight visitors' recorded experiences from the supplier's much broader promise. A product can perform well in a small trial while still needing further checks. The announcement has a commercial purpose and selects the most positive part of the report. A careful reader could ask for the original notes, look for independent testing and include more users in a local trial. Recognising this purpose helps readers judge the claim without dismissing every product detail.

items.title: Synthesise
items.prompt: What conclusion follows when both sources are considered?

stimuli.text:
Source A. Comparing Paper Covers. Jo, craft group test record, 20 October. Fictional practice source.
The craft group compared four folded covers with four patchwork covers for battery lanterns. They used the same frame size and dry paper from the same pack. An adult placed each finished cover beside the same fan for three minutes. The group recorded whether a seam opened or the paper tore. This was a classroom-style material comparison, not a safety certification.
One folded cover tore at a corner. None of the four patchwork covers tore during the short test. The record also notes that the patchwork covers took longer to assemble and used more tape. The group kept the damaged cover to examine the torn corner. Jo suggests that strengthening a fold might change the result, so the shape of a cover is not the only possible explanation.
The record describes what happened under these particular conditions. It does not test rain, strong outdoor gusts or repeated use. Four examples of each design are a small sample. The group recommends trying more covers before deciding which design is more durable. Its notes are useful because they describe materials, method and observations as well as questions. Another group could repeat the comparison and record whether its results agree. Neither design should be described as unbreakable on the strength of this test.

Source B. Lanterns That Last Forever. Promotional poster from a fictional craft seller, 21 October. Fictional practice source.
Our patchwork lantern covers never tear! A craft group tried a few paper covers near a fan and none of its patchwork examples broke. Our poster turns that short observation into a promise that every patchwork cover will last forever. The headline gives no conditions and does not mention the small number tested. It also leaves out the extra time and tape needed to make the covers.
The poster offers colourful paper packs and shows three attractive finished lanterns. It tells readers the price and how to join a workshop. It does not show the test record or explain whether the pictured covers use the same paper, tape or frame. The seller benefits if people choose the advertised design, so the purpose of the poster matters when evaluating its language.
A reader can enjoy the design without accepting an unsupported guarantee. The short test suggests a question worth investigating, but it cannot predict every future use. Rain, repeated handling and different construction methods could produce other results. Comparing the poster with the original record reveals the difference between an observed outcome and a universal claim. Asking for details and looking for further evidence are useful next steps before treating a cheerful slogan as a dependable promise.

stimuli.text:
Source A. Watching a Water Bowl. Ella, neighbourhood observation notebook, 15 October. Fictional practice source.
Ella watched a clean water bowl from the same window for ten minutes on each of five mornings. She also noted that all five mornings were warm. Her notebook does not compare warm weather with cold weather or this balcony with other locations.

She would also like to compare observations at different times of day. Her record explains what she counted and what she did not know. The author sells the product and wants readers to buy it.

Readers can separate the useful product information from the claims about bird behaviour. items.title: Argument
items.prompt: Which evidence would strengthen the broad claim?

stimuli.text:
Source A. Testing a Garden Handle. Mina and Leena, design trial notes, 18 October. Fictional practice source.
The garden team tried three temporary gate handles. Eight volunteer visitors tested each design while the gate was supervised. The team recorded whether each visitor could reach and grip the handle and whether the gate latched after use. They did not ask visitors to give a score for how attractive the handle looked.
The first design caught one person's sleeve. Two visitors found the second design difficult to grip. Everyone in this small group could reach and grip the third design. The team checked its latch three times and found it closed each time. These observations helped them choose a design for a longer trial. They did not prove that it would suit every visitor or remain reliable through every season.
The notes include a sketch and explain the testing steps. They also name two questions for later: whether rain makes the handle slippery and whether visitors using different mobility aids can use it comfortably. The volunteers were available on one afternoon, so the group might not represent all garden users. Mina and Leena recommend inviting more visitors before making a permanent change. Their report combines a useful comparison with clear limits. It gives readers enough detail to understand the decision and to suggest what should be tested next.

Source B. A Perfect Gate for Everyone. Promotional announcement from a fictional handle supplier, 19 October. Fictional practice source.
Choose our new garden handle and solve every access problem at once! A small group tried a similar design and everyone managed to use it. Our announcement therefore calls this handle perfect for every person, every gate and every kind of weather. It says no further testing is necessary because a successful afternoon tells us everything we need to know.
The announcement includes a photograph of a smiling visitor and a large button inviting readers to place an order. It lists the colour choices and price. Those details are useful when comparing products, but they do not establish the universal access claim. The supplier does not explain whether its handle has the same dimensions or mechanism as the tested model. It provides no record of use in rain or over a long period.
Readers should distinguish the eight visitors' recorded experiences from the supplier's much broader promise. A product can perform well in a small trial while still needing further checks. The announcement has a commercial purpose and selects the most positive part of the report. A careful reader could ask for the original notes, look for independent testing and include more users in a local trial. Recognising this purpose helps readers judge the claim without dismissing every product detail.

items.title: Positioning
items.prompt: How does the narrative encourage readers to view the character?

stimuli.text:
Mina noticed that the community garden gate was open. A small rabbit was nibbling the lettuce inside. She could not see the gardener. Mina closed the gate gently after guiding the rabbit outside with a trail of leaves. Then she waited beside the fence. When the gardener arrived, she explained what had happened. He thanked her for protecting the plants without frightening the rabbit.

The next Saturday, Mina returned to help plant beans. Before she started, she checked the latch. It slid into place but slipped out again when she pushed the gate. Now she understood why the rabbit had entered. The gardener, Tomas, brought a small toolbox. He showed Mina the loose screw holding the latch to the post. She held the metal plate steady while he tightened it. They tested the gate together three times. Each time it stayed shut. Mina wrote a short note asking visitors to check the latch as they left. She drew a rabbit beside the words, hoping the picture would remind people why the gate mattered.

A week later, Mina found a new problem. A visitor using a wheelchair had difficulty reaching the high latch. The visitor, Leena, could push the gate easily once it was open, but she needed someone else to let her through. Mina felt pleased with the repair until Leena explained this. A gate that kept rabbits out also needed to welcome every gardener.

Mina asked Tomas whether they could simply lower the latch. He explained that a low latch might be easy for younger children to open without an adult. They needed to consider more than one person's needs. Leena suggested a longer handle connected to the existing mechanism. Tomas sketched the idea on the back of an old seed packet. Mina measured the gate while Leena tried different handle positions using a strip of cardboard.

They made a temporary handle and invited several visitors to test it. One handle caught on a sleeve. Another was difficult to grip with wet hands. The third design had a broad, smooth loop. Visitors could reach it from different heights, and it returned securely after use. They chose that version, then tested the latch again.

Mina changed her note. Instead of only warning people about rabbits, it welcomed visitors and explained how the new handle worked. Leena added a simple drawing. Tomas placed the note where people could read it before reaching the gate.

items.title: Positioning
items.prompt: How does the narrative encourage readers to view the character?

stimuli.text:
Arun was making a lantern for the neighbourhood walk. His first paper cover tore when he pulled it over the frame. He wanted to throw it away. His sister Jo suggested using the torn paper to practise a smaller fold. Arun tried again more slowly. The new cover fitted. He saved the scraps in a box for someone else to use.

On the evening of the walk, a gust of wind lifted several decorations from the meeting table. Arun held his lantern close while Jo gathered the loose paper. A younger child named Bea stared at her empty frame. Her cover had blown into a puddle. Arun remembered the box of scraps at home. He could not fetch it before the walk began, but Jo had kept some spare pieces in her bag. Together they made a patchwork cover. Bea chose a blue triangle for the window and a yellow circle for the moon. It looked different from the other lanterns, which pleased her.

The organisers announced that the group would follow the riverside path. Arun had practised carrying his lantern along the short route behind his house. The riverside walk was longer, and the wind was stronger there. He asked whether Bea would manage with her repaired cover. Bea said she wanted to try, but she would like to stay near someone she knew.

As they walked, Arun watched the blue and yellow patches glow around the small battery light. He had wanted his own lantern to look perfect. Now he noticed how many different designs surrounded him. One had painted leaves. Another had a crooked star. An older neighbour carried a plain jar that caught reflections from every passing light.

Ben drew a simple chart with room for another week of observations.

Their neighbour Samira noticed the chart when she came to visit. She explained that birds also needed shelter from predators and a clear view of their surroundings. A bowl could be clean and full yet still be in an unsuitable place. Ella showed her the quiet corner. A tall pot partly blocked the view from one side. With an adult's help, they moved the pot away without shifting the water bowl.

stimuli.text:
Mina noticed that the community garden gate was open. A small rabbit was nibbling the lettuce inside. She could not see the gardener. Mina closed the gate gently after guiding the rabbit outside with a trail of leaves. Then she waited beside the fence. When the gardener arrived, she explained what had happened. He thanked her for protecting the plants without frightening the rabbit.

The next Saturday, Mina returned to help plant beans. Before she started, she checked the latch. It slid into place but slipped out again when she pushed the gate. Now she understood why the rabbit had entered. The gardener, Tomas, brought a small toolbox. He showed Mina the loose screw holding the latch to the post. She held the metal plate steady while he tightened it. They tested the gate together three times. Each time it stayed shut. Mina wrote a short note asking visitors to check the latch as they left. She drew a rabbit beside the words, hoping the picture would remind people why the gate mattered.

A week later, Mina found a new problem. A visitor using a wheelchair had difficulty reaching the high latch. The visitor, Leena, could push the gate easily once it was open, but she needed someone else to let her through. Mina felt pleased with the repair until Leena explained this. A gate that kept rabbits out also needed to welcome every gardener.

Mina asked Tomas whether they could simply lower the latch. He explained that a low latch might be easy for younger children to open without an adult. They needed to consider more than one person's needs. Leena suggested a longer handle connected to the existing mechanism. Tomas sketched the idea on the back of an old seed packet. Mina measured the gate while Leena tried different handle positions using a strip of cardboard.

They made a temporary handle and invited several visitors to test it. One handle caught on a sleeve. Another was difficult to grip with wet hands. The third design had a broad, smooth loop. Visitors could reach it from different heights, and it returned securely after use. They chose that version, then tested the latch again.

Mina changed her note. Instead of only warning people about rabbits, it welcomed visitors and explained how the new handle worked. Leena added a simple drawing. Tomas placed the note where people could read it before reaching the gate.

stimuli.text:
Ella put a bowl of water on the balcony during a hot week. No birds visited on the first day. Her cousin Ben thought they should move it beside the noisy doorway. Ella suggested waiting and watching instead. The next morning, a small bird landed near the quiet corner. Ella made a note of the time before refilling the bowl.

For four mornings, Ella watched from inside the window. She recorded the time, the weather and whether a bird visited. On the fourth morning, two birds arrived together. Ben wanted to announce that the bowl was a success. Ella pointed out that four days were only a small sample. They had not watched every hour, and they could not know whether the same birds returned. They decided to keep observing without disturbing the visitors. Ella asked an adult to help clean the bowl each evening and replace the water. Ben drew a simple chart with room for another week of observations.

Their neighbour Samira noticed the chart when she came to visit. She explained that birds also needed shelter from predators and a clear view of their surroundings. A bowl could be clean and full yet still be in an unsuitable place. Ella showed her the quiet corner. A tall pot partly blocked the view from one side. With an adult's help, they moved the pot away without shifting the water bowl.

The following week was cooler. Fewer birds appeared in the mornings. Ben wondered whether moving the pot had caused the change. Ella looked at the weather notes. Perhaps the birds needed less water in cooler conditions, or perhaps they were visiting at another time. Their chart could suggest questions, but it could not answer all of them. They added a short afternoon observation on the weekend.

When their class began a project about helping local wildlife, Ben wanted to use a large heading that said their balcony had saved dozens of birds. Ella disagreed. They had counted visits, not individual birds, and had no evidence that any bird had been in danger. Samira helped them choose a more accurate heading: Watching Birds at a Balcony Water Bowl. Under it, they described what they had done and what they still did not know.

At school, some classmates found the cautious title less exciting than Ben's first idea. Then they began asking questions. How often was the bowl cleaned? Was there shade? Could the same bird visit several times? Ben answered using their notes. Ella explained that their small project was useful because other people could repeat the observations and compare them.

items.title: Evidence
items.prompt: Who is the main character in “The garden gate”?

stimuli.text:
Mina noticed that the community garden gate was open. A small rabbit was nibbling the lettuce inside. She could not see the gardener. Mina closed the gate gently after guiding the rabbit outside with a trail of leaves. Then she waited beside the fence. When the gardener arrived, she explained what had happened. He thanked her for protecting the plants without frightening the rabbit.

The next Saturday, Mina returned to help plant beans. Before she started, she checked the latch. It slid into place but slipped out again when she pushed the gate. Now she understood why the rabbit had entered. The gardener, Tomas, brought a small toolbox. He showed Mina the loose screw holding the latch to the post. She held the metal plate steady while he tightened it. They tested the gate together three times. Each time it stayed shut. Mina wrote a short note asking visitors to check the latch as they left. She drew a rabbit beside the words, hoping the picture would remind people why the gate mattered.

A week later, Mina found a new problem. A visitor using a wheelchair had difficulty reaching the high latch. The visitor, Leena, could push the gate easily once it was open, but she needed someone else to let her through. Mina felt pleased with the repair until Leena explained this. A gate that kept rabbits out also needed to welcome every gardener.

Mina asked Tomas whether they could simply lower the latch. He explained that a low latch might be easy for younger children to open without an adult. They needed to consider more than one person's needs. Leena suggested a longer handle connected to the existing mechanism. Tomas sketched the idea on the back of an old seed packet. Mina measured the gate while Leena tried different handle positions using a strip of cardboard.

They made a temporary handle and invited several visitors to test it. One handle caught on a sleeve. Another was difficult to grip with wet hands. The third design had a broad, smooth loop. Visitors could reach it from different heights, and it returned securely after use. They chose that version, then tested the latch again.

Mina changed her note. Instead of only warning people about rabbits, it welcomed visitors and explained how the new handle worked. Leena added a simple drawing. Tomas placed the note where people could read it before reaching the gate.

items.explanation: The answer is Mina. Locate the matching detail in the passage.

items.prompt: Who is the main character in “The lantern walk”?

stimuli.text:
Arun was making a lantern for the neighbourhood walk. His first paper cover tore when he pulled it over the frame. He wanted to throw it away. His sister Jo suggested using the torn paper to practise a smaller fold. Arun tried again more slowly. The new cover fitted. He saved the scraps in a box for someone else to use.

On the evening of the walk, a gust of wind lifted several decorations from the meeting table. Arun held his lantern close while Jo gathered the loose paper. A younger child named Bea stared at her empty frame. Her cover had blown into a puddle. Arun remembered the box of scraps at home. He could not fetch it before the walk began, but Jo had kept some spare pieces in her bag. Together they made a patchwork cover. Bea chose a blue triangle for the window and a yellow circle for the moon. It looked different from the other lanterns, which pleased her.

The organisers announced that the group would follow the riverside path. Arun had practised carrying his lantern along the short route behind his house. The riverside walk was longer, and the wind was stronger there. He asked whether Bea would manage with her repaired cover. Bea said she wanted to try, but she would like to stay near someone she knew.

As they walked, Arun watched the blue and yellow patches glow around the small battery light. He had wanted his own lantern to look perfect. Now he noticed how many different designs surrounded him. One had painted leaves. Another had a crooked star. An older neighbour carried a plain jar that caught reflections from every passing light.

At the narrow bridge, the group slowed down. Someone behind Arun called for everyone to hurry. Jo asked them to wait while a family crossed safely. Bea held her lantern in both hands and watched the water below. Arun stood beside her rather than pulling her forward. When she was ready, they walked across at her pace.

The path ended at a small park. The organisers invited people to place their lanterns in a wide circle, leaving room for everyone to see. Bea put hers beside Arun's. A neighbour asked where she had bought the unusual cover. Bea laughed and explained how it had been made. Arun almost mentioned that his own first cover had torn, but Bea had already begun telling the story of the blue window and yellow moon.
